message:
Hi. I'm off to Lisbon next week for a three-day work trip, my first time in Portugal, and I want to travel carry-on only this time, after the airline lost my case in the spring.

Could you suggest three things to do in Lisbon on a free evening? And how do I say "thank you" in Portuguese? Is it different depending on who's saying it? And is tipping expected in restaurants there, or is that more of an American thing?

My wheeled bag measures 56 × 36 × 23 cm including the wheels and handle, and packed it weighs 9 kg. Will it meet the carry-on limit?

Also, recommend a packing approach: rolling or folding for work shirts? I need a short out-of-office message that's professional but not stiff, since most of my contacts are clients rather than colleagues. And what's a good colour for a luggage tag so it's easy to spot? I'm flying back on the Friday evening, straight after a full day of meetings, so anything that makes the return journey less stressful is welcome.

Thanks a lot.
response:
## Three things to do on a free evening

1. **Watch sunset from a miradouro (viewpoint), then wander Alfama.** Miradouro da Senhora do Monte has the widest view, and Santa Luzia is right in Alfama. Afterwards, walk down through Alfama's lanes for dinner.
2. **Hear fado.** This is Portugal's signature music, best heard in a small *casa de fado* in Alfama or Mouraria. Booking ahead is wise, and many places include dinner, so it can double as your evening meal.
3. **Eat in Bairro Alto or Príncipe Real.** Bairro Alto gets lively after about 10 pm with small bars and street drinking. Príncipe Real is calmer and more upscale. If you're short on time, the Time Out Market at Cais do Sodré lets you try lots of dishes in one place.

## Saying "thank you"

Yes, it depends on who's speaking, not who you're thanking:
- **Obrigado** (oh-bree-GAH-doo) if you're a man.
- **Obrigada** (oh-bree-GAH-dah) if you're a woman.

**Muito obrigado/a** means "thank you very much." People will appreciate either.

## Tipping

Tipping is not expected the way it is in the US, and service charges are rarely added. Rounding up or leaving about 5–10% for good table service is appreciated but optional. In cafés, leaving the small change is plenty.

Bread, olives or cheese placed on the table when you sit down (the *couvert*) are charged if you eat them. You can send them back if you don't want them.

## Will your bag fit?

**It depends on the airline, and with several common ones it won't.** Your bag is 56 × 36 × 23 cm and weighs 9 kg. Typical limits as I understand them (they change, so check your booking):

| Airline | Cabin bag limit | Your bag |
|---|---|---|
| TAP Air Portugal | 55 × 40 × 20 cm, 8 kg | Too long by 1 cm, too deep by 3 cm, 1 kg over |
| Ryanair (Priority) | 55 × 40 × 20 cm, 10 kg | Too long and too deep |
| easyJet (large cabin bag, paid add-on) | 56 × 45 × 25 cm, 15 kg | Fits |
| British Airways | 56 × 45 × 25 cm, 23 kg | Fits |

The depth of 23 cm is the main problem on airlines with a 20 cm limit. Squeezing the bag rarely helps, because wheels and frames don't compress. If you tell me your airline I can check the specifics. Otherwise, look up the exact limit on your booking before you pack. After your lost case in the spring, the last thing you want is a forced gate-check.

## Packing work shirts

**Fold them, don't roll them.** Rolling suits t-shirts, knitwear and casual clothes. Collared shirts crease less when folded flat.

- Button the shirts, fold them around a stiff piece of card or with tissue paper between them, and lay them flat on top.
- Alternatively, interleave them so each one cushions the next.
- Hang them up as soon as you arrive. Steam from a hot shower clears most creases.
- A small travel steamer, or the hotel iron, can rescue a key shirt on the Friday.

## Out-of-office message

> Thank you for your email. I'm travelling for work from [date] to [date] with limited access to email, and will reply when I'm back on [date]. If your message is urgent, please contact [name] at [email/phone], who will be glad to help.
>
> Kind regards,
> [Name]

## Luggage tag colour

Pick something **bright and unusual**, such as fluorescent yellow, lime green or neon orange. Avoid black, navy and red, which almost everyone uses.

Even flying carry-on only, a tag is worth having in case your bag is gate-checked on a full flight. A matching strap or ribbon on the handle helps too.

## Making the Friday return easier

- **Pack Thursday night,** leaving out only the outfit for Friday, a toiletries bag and chargers.
- **Check in online** and download your boarding pass on Thursday.
- **Ask the hotel to hold your bag** after checkout if you can't take it to meetings. Most will.
- **Leave plenty of time.** Lisbon airport is close to the centre, about 20–30 minutes by taxi, Uber or Bolt, or take the metro red line. Friday evening traffic and the airport's busy security can be slow, so aim to arrive about 2 hours before departure.
- **Keep your liquids bag ready at the top** of your bag, and wear shoes that are easy to remove.
- **Carry a small "personal item" bag** (laptop bag or tote) holding your essentials: passport, chargers, medication and a change of shirt. That way, if your wheeled bag does get gate-checked, nothing you need is in it.

Have a good trip, and boa viagem!
